newsitem.title: CHINA: China to ship food aid to North Korea.
newsitem.headline: China to ship food aid to North Korea.

text.p: China said on Saturday it would donate 70,000 tonnes of grain to North Korea to help its communist neighbour overcome severe food shortages.
China's ambassador to North Korea, Wan Yongxiang, advised the Pyongyang government of the decision to start shipments in the near future, state television said.

"In order to further consolidate the traditional friendly relations between the two countries and in consideration of the actual conditions in Korea, the Chinese government has decided to donate another 70,000 tonnes of grain in the near future," television said.
"The Chinese government and people express their deep sympathy for Korea's current grain problems."
North Korea, hit by floods and failed harvests, is on the brink of starvation, international aid workers say.
The U.N. World Food Programme has appealed for $95.5 million for 200,000 tonnes of food for North Korea, well short of what is needed to stave off famine.

Pyongyang officials have demanded substantial food aid before joining talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China aimed at securing a lasting peace to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
China's state television made no mention of any talks.
But it pointed out that no payments were expected in return for the grain and this was not the first such act of charity.
Top U.S. defence officials on Friday cautioned against rushing to help North Korea, saying the nation was on a war footing despite its appeals for food to avert famine.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, during a visit to South Korea, portrayed a repressive North Korean government cynically begging for food while pouring scarce resources into a military ready to strike its southern neighbour.
He made clear large-scale assistance was unlikely unless Pyongyang began dismantling its military machine and showed it was ready to repay food with goodwill peace gestures.
China fought alongside the North in the Korean War but it has been forced to balance ties to its communist ally with its growing friendship for the capitalist South.
Its bonds to North Korea were badly strained when senior Pyongyang official Hwang Jang-yop sought asylum in South Korea's diplomatic mission in Beijing in February.
Hwang was allowed to leave for the Philippines after a standoff that lasted nearly five weeks.
